subject: heart
title: Heart Engineering: Two Pumps and a Timing System
summary: Circuits, valves, and the electrical delay that makes each beat work.

keys.prompt: Why does the heart's signal pause at the AV node on every beat?
keys.answer: So the ventricles can finish filling with blood before they contract.

keys.prompt: Why is the heart called "two pumps in one"?
keys.answer: The right side pumps oxygen-poor blood to the lungs; the left side pumps oxygen-rich blood to the whole body.

keys.prompt: How do you turn a 30-second pulse count into a heart rate, and what's normal at rest?
keys.answer: Double the count to get beats per minute. At rest, 60 to 100 is normal.

cards.title: A pump with a built-in delay
cards.text: Your heart has a timing system that deliberately slows its own electrical signal for a split second on every beat. Why would a pump want a delay?

cards.question: Your heart slows its own electrical signal for a split second on every beat. Why would a pump want a delay?

options.text: To let the heart muscle rest between beats
To let the lower chambers finish filling before they squeeze
To keep the heartbeat from getting too loud

cards.reveal: It's for filling. The signal slows at the AV node, which gives the ventricles time to finish filling before they contract. The delay is a feature, not a bug.

cards.title: Two pumps in one
cards.text: The right side sends oxygen-poor blood to the lungs. The left side sends oxygen-rich blood to the whole body. The left ventricle makes the high pressure needed to push blood all the way through your body.

why.q: Why does the left ventricle need more pressure than the right?
why.a: The left side has to push blood all the way through your body. The right side sends it to the lungs.

cards.title: The route
cards.text: Body → vena cava → right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary veins → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta → body. Four valves keep it moving one way.
cards.example: Even the heart muscle needs its own blood supply: coronary arteries branch off the aorta to feed it.

cards.title: The timing system
cards.text: Each beat starts in the SA node, the natural pacemaker in the right atrium. The signal spreads through the atria, which squeeze blood into the ventricles. At the AV node, the signal slows down slightly. That gives the ventricles time to finish filling before they contract.

cards.title: Measure it
cards.text: Find your pulse at the wrist, count beats for 30 seconds, and double it. At rest, 60 to 100 beats per minute is normal. During a soccer sprint, your rate rises to get more oxygen to your muscles.
cards.example: Math: at 60 to 100 beats per minute, that is 86,400 to 144,000 beats a day.

cards.question: Your heart rate goes up when you exercise and down when you rest, and that is a sign of a heart responding well. How could an athlete use heart-rate data to train smarter? What could it miss?
nudges: What does a lower resting rate over time suggest?
What can't a single number tell you?

questions.q: Why does the signal slow down at the AV node?

options.text: So the ventricles can finish filling before they contract
options.why: Right. The delay is a feature, not a bug.

options.text: Because the AV node is broken
options.why: In a healthy heart the slowdown is normal and useful.

options.text: To make the heart beat faster
options.why: It adds a brief delay within each beat.

questions.q: Which chamber pumps blood out to the whole body?

options.why: It generates the high pressure needed to reach your whole body.
The right atrium collects oxygen-poor blood coming back from the body.
The right ventricle pumps blood to the lungs.

questions.q: You count 38 beats in 30 seconds. What is your heart rate?

options.why: 38 × 2 = 76, which is in the normal resting range.
You double the count, not halve it.
